n: Laban’s sons complain that Jacob has grown rich at their father’s expense. Jealousy is turning the household against Jacob.
Jacob notices that Laban’s attitude toward him has changed. The relationship has soured.
The Lord tells Jacob to return home and promises, “I will be with thee”—the same promise made at Bethel.
Jacob calls Rachel and Leah out to the field, where they can speak privately.

f.g: Away from Laban’s household, to talk in private.

n: Jacob explains that Laban has turned against him, but God has stayed with him.

f.w: the God of my father hath been with me

n: Jacob reminds his wives how hard he has worked for their father.
Laban cheated him by changing his wages again and again, but God protected him.

f.g: A Hebrew expression meaning “many times” or “over and over.”

n: Whatever terms Laban set, the flocks produced in Jacob’s favor. God overruled Laban’s schemes.
Jacob gives God the credit for transferring Laban’s flocks to him.

f.w: God hath taken away the cattle of your father
f.g: Jacob sees God’s hand, not his own cleverness, behind his wealth.

n: Jacob recounts a dream at breeding time showing the rams were striped and spotted.
The angel of God called Jacob by name, and he answered, “Here am I,” like Abraham before him.
The angel showed Jacob that God had seen Laban’s mistreatment and was blessing Jacob’s flock. The striped branches of chapter 30 were not the real cause.

f.w: I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee

n: God identifies Himself as the God of Bethel, reminding Jacob of his vow there, and tells him to go home.
Rachel and Leah agree: there is nothing left for them in their father’s house. For once the sisters speak with one voice.

f.g: A share of the family estate.

n: They complain that Laban treated them like foreigners, “selling” them and using up the bride-price that should have benefited them.

f.g: Spent the wealth (from Jacob’s labor) that should have been their dowry.

n: They affirm that the wealth God gave Jacob belongs to them and their children, and they urge him to obey God.

f.w: whatsoever God hath said unto thee, do

n: Jacob loads his family onto camels.
He takes all the livestock and property he earned in Paddan-aram and sets off to his father Isaac in Canaan.
While Laban is away shearing sheep, Rachel steals her father’s household idols. These figurines may have represented family gods or even claims to inheritance.

f.g: Hebrew teraphim—household idols or figurines, perhaps tied to family protection or inheritance rights.
Sheep-shearing was a busy, festive time that took the men away.

n: Jacob slips away without telling Laban.

f.g: Literally “stole the heart of”—deceived; left secretly.

n: Jacob crosses the Euphrates and heads toward the hill country of Gilead, east of the Jordan.

f.g: A hilly, wooded region east of the Jordan River.

n: Laban learns on the third day that Jacob has fled.
Laban gathers his relatives and chases Jacob for seven days, catching up in Gilead.
God warns Laban in a dream not to say anything to Jacob, good or bad. God protects Jacob as promised.

f.g: An idiom: do nothing at all to harm him.

n: Laban catches up, and both camps pitch tents in the hills of Gilead.

f.g: Set up camp in the hill country.

n: Laban accuses Jacob of carrying off his daughters like prisoners of war.
He claims he would have sent them off with a farewell celebration—music, songs, tambourines, and harps. His claim of warm intentions sounds hollow.
Laban complains that he did not even get to kiss his grandchildren goodbye.
Laban admits he could hurt Jacob but that Jacob’s God warned him not to. God’s protection is acknowledged even by Laban.
Laban understands Jacob’s homesickness—but why steal his gods? The irony is clear: what kind of gods can be stolen?
Jacob explains that he left secretly because he feared Laban would take his daughters by force.
Not knowing Rachel took the idols, Jacob rashly declares that whoever has them shall die. His words create real danger for Rachel.

f.g: A rash oath that puts Rachel at risk.

n: Laban searches every tent—Jacob’s, Leah’s, the maidservants’—and finally Rachel’s.

f.g: The tents of Bilhah and Zilpah.

n: Rachel has hidden the idols in her camel saddle and is sitting on them. Laban searches everything but finds nothing.

f.g: The camel saddle, often a basket-like seat.

n: Rachel tells her father she cannot stand because she is having her period. Laban’s precious gods are being sat upon—a mocking picture of idols.
Jacob angrily confronts Laban, demanding to know what crime justified such a pursuit.
Jacob challenges Laban to display anything he found before both families, to judge between them.
Jacob describes twenty years of faithful service: Laban’s animals did not miscarry under his care, and he never ate Laban’s rams.
Jacob even covered the losses when wild animals killed sheep—going beyond what custom required of a shepherd.
Jacob endured burning heat by day, freezing cold by night, and lost sleep. A shepherd’s life was hard and dangerous.

f.w: my sleep departed from mine eyes

n: Twenty years: fourteen for his wives, six for flocks, with wages changed again and again.

f.w: fourteen years for thy two daughters

n: If not for God—the God of Abraham and “the Fear of Isaac”—Jacob would have left empty-handed. God saw his hardship and rebuked Laban.

f.g: A unique name for God: the One whom Isaac revered.

n: Laban claims everything is still his but admits he can do nothing. He then proposes a treaty.

f.w: all that thou seest is mine
f.g: Laban’s possessive attitude to the end.

n: Laban suggests a covenant to serve as a witness between them.

f.g: A lasting testimony of their agreement.

n: Jacob sets up a stone as a pillar, as he did at Bethel.

f.w: set it up for a pillar

n: Jacob’s relatives gather stones into a heap, and they eat a covenant meal there.

f.g: A pile of stones—a boundary marker and memorial.

n: Laban names the heap in Aramaic, and Jacob in Hebrew; both mean “heap of witness.” The two languages hint at two peoples—Arameans and Israelites.

f.g: Hebrew for “heap of witness”; sounds like Gilead.

n: Laban declares the heap a witness between them.
The place is also called Mizpah, “watchtower.” Laban’s words—“The LORD watch between me and thee”—were a warning, though today they are often used as a tender farewell.
Laban warns Jacob not to mistreat his daughters or marry other wives. God will be witness even when no one else is.
Laban points to the heap and pillar.

f.g: Laban claims credit for setting them up.

n: The heap and pillar mark a boundary neither will cross to harm the other—a peace treaty.
Laban calls on the God of Abraham and Nahor; Jacob swears by “the Fear of Isaac,” the God his father worshipped.

f.g: Laban may mean a family god distinct from Jacob’s God.

f.w: the fear of his father Isaac

n: Jacob offers a sacrifice and shares a meal with his relatives. They spend the night on the mountain.

f.g: Covenant sacrifice and meal sealed the agreement.

n: Early the next morning Laban kisses and blesses his daughters and grandchildren and goes home. Jacob is finally free to return to Canaan.

f.g: Laban exits the story for good.
